name: Chole (Chana Masala)

ingredients.name: Black tea bag (optional, for the dark colour)
ingredients.householdMeasure: 1 bag (or 1 tsp tea leaves tied in muslin)

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.householdMeasure: 1 small-medium tomato, finely chopped or grated

ingredients.name: Dry mango powder (amchur) (optional, only if your chole masala is not tangy)

equipment: Kadai or a heavy pan (about 20 cm) for the masala
Wooden spoon or flat spatula, plus a ladle or the back of a steel spoon to mash a few chickpeas
Measuring spoons and a ¼ cup measure

steps.title: The night before, measure ¼ cup (50 g) dried chickpeas into a bowl
steps.text: The night before, measure ¼ cup (50 g) dried chickpeas into a bowl
steps.visualCue: a small heap of beige chickpeas
steps.cameraCheck: the chickpeas in the bowl
steps.videoShot: chickpeas pouring from the measuring cup into the bowl
steps.watchOut: a heaped cup, which gives too much chole for one serving; level the cup with a knife.

steps.title: Rinse the chickpeas 2 times in water and drain
steps.text: Rinse the chickpeas 2 times in water and drain
steps.tip: throw away any shrivelled or black chickpeas that float.
steps.visualCue: the water runs clear and any dust or broken husks float off
steps.cameraCheck: the rinsed chickpeas
steps.videoShot: a hand swirling chickpeas in water
steps.watchOut: stones or black, shrivelled chickpeas hiding in the batch; pick them out before soaking.

steps.title: Cover the chickpeas with 250 ml (1 cup) water and leave them to soak for 8–10 hours (overnight)
steps.text: Cover the chickpeas with 250 ml (1 cup) water and leave them to soak for 8–10 hours (overnight)
steps.tip: in hot Mumbai weather, soak in the fridge if it will be more than 10 hours, so the water does not turn sour.
steps.visualCue: next morning the chickpeas have roughly doubled in size and look plump and smooth
steps.cameraCheck: the soaked chickpeas next to the bowl's water line
steps.videoShot: a before/after of the bowl, dry versus swollen chickpeas
steps.watchOut: a sour smell or foam on the water, which means the soak ran too warm or too long; in Mumbai heat, soak in the fridge, and bin the batch if it smells off.

steps.title: Drain the soaking water and put the chickpeas into the pressure cooker with 300 ml fresh water
steps.text: Drain the soaking water and put the chickpeas into the pressure cooker with 300 ml fresh water
steps.visualCue: water about 3 cm above the chickpeas
steps.cameraCheck: the open cooker with chickpeas and water
steps.videoShot: water poured over the chickpeas in the cooker
steps.watchOut: too little water, which makes the cooker run dry and scorch; add 50 ml if the level is below the chickpeas.

steps.title: Add 1 black tea bag and ¼ tsp of the salt, then close the lid
steps.text: Add 1 black tea bag and ¼ tsp of the salt, then close the lid
steps.tip: the tea only adds colour, not taste. Skip it if you don't mind a lighter, golden chole.
steps.visualCue: the tea bag floating on top
steps.cameraCheck: the tea bag in the cooker before closing
steps.videoShot: the tea bag dropped in and the lid locked
steps.watchOut: a tea bag that bursts in the cooker and leaves tea leaves in the chickpeas (one recipe site warns about this); remove the staple, or tie 1 tsp tea leaves in a muslin pouch instead.

steps.title: Pressure cook on medium heat for 6–7 whistles (about 18 min), then turn off the heat and let the pressure drop on its own
steps.text: Pressure cook on medium heat for 6–7 whistles (about 18 min), then turn off the heat and let the pressure drop on its own
steps.tip: never force the lid open while there is still pressure.
steps.visualCue: whistles counted, then the valve drops and the hissing stops
steps.cameraCheck: the closed cooker on the flame
steps.videoShot: the cooker whistling
steps.watchOut: forcing the lid open early (dangerous) or counting too few whistles; sources range from 3 to 6 whistles for soaked chickpeas, so the softness check in step 11 decides.

steps.title: Finely chop 1 small onion (60 g)
steps.text: Finely chop 1 small onion (60 g)
steps.visualCue: small even pieces about the size of a rice grain
steps.cameraCheck: the chopped onion on the board
steps.videoShot: knife chopping the onion
steps.watchOut: big, uneven pieces, which stay raw-tasting; chop smaller than you think.

steps.title: Finely chop or grate 1 small-medium tomato (75 g)
steps.text: Finely chop or grate 1 small-medium tomato (75 g)
steps.visualCue: juicy pulp or small cubes, with skin left behind if grated
steps.cameraCheck: the tomato in a bowl
steps.videoShot: tomato rubbed on the grater
steps.watchOut: tomato skin curling into the gravy; if grating, stop when only the skin is left in your hand.

steps.title: Grate ¾ inch ginger (4 g) and finely chop 3 garlic cloves (6 g)
steps.text: Grate ¾ inch ginger (4 g) and finely chop 3 garlic cloves (6 g)
steps.visualCue: a small pile of each
steps.cameraCheck: the ginger and garlic piles
steps.videoShot: ginger on the grater, then garlic chopped
steps.watchOut: big garlic pieces that stay raw; chop fine or crush them.

steps.title: Slit 1 green chilli lengthwise and chop 1 tbsp coriander leaves
steps.text: Slit 1 green chilli lengthwise and chop 1 tbsp coriander leaves
steps.visualCue: chilli split open, coriander finely chopped
steps.cameraCheck: chilli and coriander on the board
steps.videoShot: knife slitting the chilli
steps.watchOut: chilli on your fingers, which burns your eyes later; wash your hands before touching your face.

steps.title: Open the cooker, lift out and throw away the tea bag, and check that the chickpeas are soft
steps.text: Open the cooker, lift out and throw away the tea bag, and check that the chickpeas are soft
steps.tip: if they are still firm, add 50 ml water and cook 2–3 more whistles. Under-cooked chickpeas never soften in the masala.
steps.visualCue: a chickpea squashes easily between your thumb and finger, with no hard or chalky centre
steps.cameraCheck: a chickpea pressed flat between two fingers
steps.videoShot: the dark-brown chickpeas, and a fingertip squashing one
steps.watchOut: firm chickpeas, which never soften in the masala; if one is still firm, add 50 ml water, close the lid and cook 2–3 more whistles.

steps.title: Strain the chickpeas, keeping all the cooking liquid in a cup
steps.text: Strain the chickpeas, keeping all the cooking liquid in a cup
steps.visualCue: about 150–200 ml of brown stock saved
steps.cameraCheck: the cup of stock and the strained chickpeas
steps.videoShot: liquid pouring through the strainer into a cup
steps.watchOut: pouring the stock down the sink; you need 150 ml of it in step 21. Strain over a cup.

steps.title: Heat 2 tsp (10 g) oil in a kadai on medium heat
steps.text: Heat 2 tsp (10 g) oil in a kadai on medium heat
steps.visualCue: the oil shimmers and flows easily
steps.cameraCheck: hot oil in the kadai
steps.videoShot: oil swirled around the pan
steps.watchOut: smoking oil, which tastes bitter (mustard oil should be heated until it just smokes, then cooled slightly); lower the heat if it smokes hard.

steps.title: Add ½ tsp cumin seeds and 1 bay leaf, and let them crackle
steps.text: Add ½ tsp cumin seeds and 1 bay leaf, and let them crackle
steps.visualCue: cumin sizzles and turns a shade darker, with a nutty smell
steps.cameraCheck: cumin and bay leaf in the oil
steps.videoShot: close-up of cumin bubbling
steps.watchOut: black, bitter cumin from waiting too long; add the onion as soon as the seeds darken.

steps.title: Add the chopped onion and sauté until golden brown
steps.text: Add the chopped onion and sauté until golden brown
steps.tip: well-browned onion gives chole its deep colour and taste. If it starts sticking, add 1 tbsp water and keep stirring.
steps.visualCue: the onion is evenly golden brown (darker than for dal), soft and sweet-smelling
steps.cameraCheck: the golden-brown onion
steps.videoShot: onion stirred in the kadai, slowly colouring
steps.watchOut: pale onion, which gives a thin, raw-tasting chole, or burnt black edges, which turn it bitter; add 1 tbsp water if it starts sticking and keep stirring.

steps.title: Add the ginger, garlic and green chilli, and sauté
steps.text: Add the ginger, garlic and green chilli, and sauté
steps.visualCue: the raw garlic smell is gone
steps.cameraCheck: the pan with aromatics mixed in
steps.videoShot: aromatics tossed into the onion
steps.watchOut: browned garlic, which turns bitter; move to the next step at the first golden edge.

steps.title: Lower the heat and add ⅛ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1 tsp coriander powder, then stir for 20 seconds
steps.text: Lower the heat and add ⅛ tsp turmeric, ½ tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and 1 tsp coriander powder, then stir for 20 seconds
steps.tip: if the pan looks dry, splash in 1 tbsp of the chickpea stock so the spices do not burn.
steps.visualCue: the spices smell toasted and coat the onion
steps.cameraCheck: the spiced onion
steps.videoShot: powders sprinkled in and stirred
steps.watchOut: burnt powders (a sharp, acrid smell and dark specks); take the pan off the flame and splash in 1 tbsp of chickpea stock.

steps.title: Add the tomato and a pinch of salt, raise the heat to medium, and cook until the masala is thick and oil shows at the edges
steps.text: Add the tomato and a pinch of salt, raise the heat to medium, and cook until the masala is thick and oil shows at the edges
steps.visualCue: the tomato melts into a thick paste and tiny oil drops appear at the edges
steps.cameraCheck: the masala with oil separating
steps.videoShot: the spatula pressing the masala and oil seeping out
steps.watchOut: a sharp, raw tomato smell and no oil at the edges, which means it needs more time; keep cooking and pressing the tomato.

steps.title: Add 1 tsp chole masala (and ¼ tsp amchur if using) and stir for 30 seconds
steps.text: Add 1 tsp chole masala (and ¼ tsp amchur if using) and stir for 30 seconds
steps.visualCue: the masala turns darker brown and smells tangy and spicy
steps.cameraCheck: the dark masala
steps.videoShot: chole masala sprinkled over the base
steps.watchOut: scorching the powder; stir constantly and move on at 30 seconds.

steps.title: Add the boiled chickpeas and stir to coat them in the masala
steps.text: Add the boiled chickpeas and stir to coat them in the masala
steps.visualCue: every chickpea is coated brown
steps.cameraCheck: the coated chickpeas in the kadai
steps.videoShot: chickpeas tipped in and folded through
steps.watchOut: white, uncoated chickpeas at the bottom of the pan; keep folding until all look brown.

steps.title: Pour in 150 ml of the saved chickpea stock (top up with water if short) and stir
steps.text: Pour in 150 ml of the saved chickpea stock (top up with water if short) and stir
steps.visualCue: the chickpeas are just covered by a loose, dark gravy
steps.cameraCheck: the gravy level in the kadai
steps.videoShot: brown stock poured into the masala
steps.watchOut: too much liquid, which gives a watery chole; add 150 ml, not more, as it thickens later.

steps.title: Add the remaining salt (about ¼ tsp, to taste) and bring to a boil
steps.text: Add the remaining salt (about ¼ tsp, to taste) and bring to a boil
steps.visualCue: bubbles across the surface
steps.cameraCheck: the bubbling chole
steps.videoShot: the gravy coming to a boil
steps.watchOut: over-salting, especially with canned chickpeas or a salty chole masala; taste the gravy first and add a pinch at a time.

steps.title: Mash 6–8 chickpeas against the side of the kadai with the back of the ladle
steps.text: Mash 6–8 chickpeas against the side of the kadai with the back of the ladle
steps.tip: this is how restaurants get a thick gravy without cream or cashew.
steps.visualCue: a few crushed chickpeas mixing into the gravy and making it thicker
steps.cameraCheck: the mashed chickpeas at the side of the pan
steps.videoShot: ladle pressing chickpeas flat against the kadai
steps.watchOut: mashing too many, which turns the chole into a paste; stop at 6–8.

steps.title: Lower the heat, partly cover, and simmer, stirring every 2 minutes
steps.text: Lower the heat, partly cover, and simmer, stirring every 2 minutes
steps.tip: chole thickens more as it stands, so stop while it is slightly looser than you want.
steps.visualCue: the gravy thickens and clings to the chickpeas, but still flows off the spoon
steps.cameraCheck: a spoonful of gravy lifted from the pan
steps.videoShot: thick gravy dripping slowly from the ladle
steps.watchOut: gravy sticking and burning at the bottom (a burnt smell); stir from the bottom and add 2 tbsp hot water if it gets too thick.

steps.title: Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi between your palms over the kadai and stir it in
steps.text: Crush 1 tsp kasuri methi between your palms over the kadai and stir it in
steps.visualCue: green-brown flecks in the gravy and a strong fenugreek aroma
steps.cameraCheck: the kasuri methi falling into the pan
steps.videoShot: palms rubbing kasuri methi over the chole
steps.watchOut: adding kasuri methi too early or boiling it, which makes it bitter; add it only at the end.

steps.title: Turn off the heat, remove the bay leaf, and stir in most of the coriander leaves
steps.text: Turn off the heat, remove the bay leaf, and stir in most of the coriander leaves
steps.visualCue: green flecks through the dark chole
steps.cameraCheck: the finished pan
steps.videoShot: coriander stirred through
steps.watchOut: leaving the bay leaf in; it is not eaten, so fish it out.

steps.title: Ladle the chole into a bowl, and top with the rest of the coriander and 1 tsp lemon juice if you like
steps.text: Ladle the chole into a bowl, and top with the rest of the coriander and 1 tsp lemon juice if you like
steps.visualCue: a glossy, deep-brown bowl of chickpeas in thick gravy
steps.cameraCheck: the final plated chole
steps.videoShot: chole ladled into the bowl and garnished (hero shot)
steps.watchOut: lemon added in the hot pan, which dulls the colour; squeeze it on the bowl at the end.

reasons: the home version is a high-fibre (about 11 g), plant-protein (about 13 g) dish made with 2 tsp oil, no frying, no cream and no added sugar. Restaurant chole is usually made with 1.5–3 tbsp oil or ghee plus a ghee or butter finish, more salt, and sometimes cashew or cream. It is also often ordered with fried bhaturas, which can more than double the meal's calories.

researchRating.basis: chole is one of North India's best-loved dishes and a fixture of Mumbai's Punjabi restaurants and chole bhature joints. The strongest rating re-checked this run is Hebbar's Kitchen pindi chole at 4.99/5 from 266 votes; smaller pages vary (Zayka Ka Tadka Punjabi chole 3.5/5 from 35 ratings; Cooking From Heart 5/5 from only 2 votes), and small samples were not weighted. It loses a little because the overnight soak and long cooking put some people off for weeknights.

storage: Fridge: safe for 3 days in an airtight container. It often tastes better the next day. Freezer: up to 2–3 months. Boiled, drained plain chickpeas also freeze well for up to 3 months, which makes the next batch a 25-minute dish. Reheating: add 2–4 tbsp water because the gravy thickens. Heat on the stove until it bubbles, or microwave for 1.5–2 min, stirring halfway.
leftoverRemix: make chole tikki chaat. Mash leftover boiled potato into aloo tikkis and pan-fry them in 1 tsp oil, then top with warm leftover chole, whisked curd, green and tamarind chutneys, chopped onion, sev and chaat masala. Alternatively, mash the chole a little thicker and stuff it into a wholewheat wrap with onion and mint chutney for a chole roll.
burnOff: Running: about 5 km at about 70 kcal per km. Walking: about 7 km at a brisk pace (est.), using about 50 kcal per km. With 2 rotis (about 580 kcal total): about 8.3 km running or about 11.5 km walking (est.).

navratri.reason: chickpeas are a pulse and the recipe uses onion, garlic and chole masala, none of which fit the most common vrat rule set (assumption: grains and pulses avoided)

ekadashi.reason: pulses are avoided on Ekadashi in most families (assumption), and onion and garlic are used

jain.reason: drop onion, garlic and fresh ginger (roots); use extra tomato, hing and sonth (see Jain variant)

ramadan.reason: vegetarian, so no halal-meat issue; about 13.5 g protein and 11 g fibre keep you full for sehri, but the dish is salty (about 1,000 mg sodium, est.), so use a pinch less salt for sehri

jain.reason: drop onion 60 g, garlic 6 g and fresh ginger 4 g (all roots, Patch 05); use extra tomato, hing and a pinch of sonth (dry ginger powder) instead, and check the chole masala label for onion or garlic powder (see Jain variant)

vegan.reason: chickpeas, oil, vegetables and spices only; no dairy, ghee, honey or egg

pescatarian.reason: vegetarian recipe with no meat or egg

sattvik.reason: skip onion 60 g and garlic 6 g (fresh ginger can stay); brown extra tomato and add hing instead (see Sattvik variant)

glutenFree.reason: no wheat, rava, maida or hing in the recipe; check the store-bought chole masala label, because blends can contain compounded hing (which usually carries wheat flour)

dairyFree.reason: no dairy in the recipe (oil, not ghee or butter)

variants.reason: main recipe already vegan (oil, not ghee or butter).
main recipe already gluten-free; use a chole masala labelled without wheat or compounded hing.
